body_md: Let Assumptions \ref{A_1}--\ref{A_3} and \ref{B} hold. For any $k\in{\mathbb N}\cup\{0\}$ arbitrarily fixed, Problem \eqref{IS}, Problem \eqref{OS}, and Problem \eqref{ES} are well-posed in the sense of Definition \ref{2.2.1}, Definition \ref{2.2.2}, and  Definition \ref{2.2.3}, respectively.

title: Proof
body_md:
Proposition \ref{Pr A.1} shows that the choice of boundary conditions at each iterative step makes sense.
    By applying the Lax-Milgram lemma (see Theorem 3.1.4 in \cite{kesavan}), we obtain the well-posedness of Problem \eqref{IS}--\eqref{ES}.

title: Proof
body_md:
The following identity holds for all $k\in{\mathbb N} \cup \{0\}$:
     egin{align*}
    &\|
abla e^{(2k)}\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2- \|
abla e^{(2k+1)}\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2\&= \|
abla e^{(2k)}\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2- \|
abla e^{(2k)}-
abla(e^{(2k)}-e^{(2k+1)})\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2\
    &= \|
abla e^{(2k)}\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2- \|
abla e^{(2k)}\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+2\underset{\Omega}{\int}
abla e^{(2k)}
abla (e^{(2k)}-e^{(2k+1)}){\,	extrm d}x\
    &\hspace{4mm}- \|
abla (e^{(2k)}-e^{(2k+1)})\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2\
    &=2\underset{\Omega}{\int}
abla e^{(2k)}
abla (e^{(2k)}-e^{(2k+1)}){\,	extrm d}x- \|
abla (e^{(2k)}-e^{(2k+1)})\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2.
\end{align*}
This implies that
 egin{equation}
    egin{aligned}\label{12}
       & \|
abla e^{(2k)}\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2- \|
abla e^{(2k+1)}\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2\
       &=2\underset{\Omega}{\int}
abla e^{(2k)}
abla (e^{(2k)}-e^{(2k+1)}){\,	extrm d}x- \|
abla (e^{(2k)}-e^{(2k+1)})\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2.
   \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Reformulating the last term of \eqref{12} by applying Green's formula, and using the facts that  $e^{(2k)}-e^{(2k+1)}=0$ on $L$ and $ rac{\partial e^{(2k+1)}}{\partial n}=0$ on $S$, we obtain
 egin{align*}
    &2\underset{\Omega}{\int}
abla e^{(2k)}
abla (e^{(2k)}-e^{(2k+1)}){\,	extrm d}x- \|
abla (e^{(2k)}-e^{(2k+1)})\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2\
    &=2\underset{S}{\int} rac{\partial e^{(2k)}}{\partial n}(e^{(2k)}-e^{(2k+1)}){\,	extrm d}\sigma-\|
abla (e^{(2k)}-e^{(2k+1)})\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2\
    &=2\underset{S}{\int} rac{\partial}{\partial n}(e^{(2k)}-e^{(2k+1)})(e^{(2k)}-e^{(2k+1)}){\,	extrm d}\sigma-\|
abla (e^{(2k)}-e^{(2k+1)})\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2\
    &=2\underset{\Omega}{\int}|
abla(e^{(2k)}-e^{(2k+1)})|^2{\,	extrm d}x-\|
abla (e^{(2k)}-e^{(2k+1)})\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2\
    &=\|
abla (e^{(2k)}-e^{(2k+1)})\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2.
\end{align*}
Hence, for all $k\in {\mathbb N}\cup\{0\}$, we obtain the first key identity
 egin{equation}\label{13}
    \|
abla e^{(2k)}\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2- \|
abla e^{(2k+1)}\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2=\|
abla (e^{(2k)}-e^{(2k+1)})\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2.
\end{equation}
Proceeding similarly, for all $k\in {\mathbb N}\cup\{0\}$ we have
 egin{align*}
   &\|
abla e^{(2k+1)}\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2- \|
abla e^{(2k+2)}\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2\
    &= \|
abla e^{(2k+1)}\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2- \|
abla e^{(2k+1)}-
abla(e^{(2k+1)}-e^{(2k+2)})\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2\
    &= \|
abla e^{(2k+1)}\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2- \|
abla e^{(2k+1)}\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+2\underset{\Omega}{\int}
abla e^{(2k+1)}
abla (e^{(2k+1)}-e^{(2k+2)}){\,	extrm d}x\
    &\hspace{4mm}- \|
abla (e^{(2k+1)}-e^{(2k+2)})\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2\
    &=2\underset{\Omega}{\int}
abla e^{(2k+1)}
abla (e^{(2k+1)}-e^{(2k+2)}){\,	extrm d}x- \|
abla (e^{(2k+1)}-e^{(2k+2)})\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2,
\end{align*}
since $ rac{\partial}{\partial n} (e^{(2k+1)}-e^{(2k+2)})=0$ on $L$, and $e^{(2k+2)}=0$ on $S$, we consequently obtain 
 egin{align*}
     & 2\underset{\Omega}{\int}
abla e^{(2k+1)}
abla (e^{(2k+1)}-e^{(2k+2)}){\,	extrm d}x- \|
abla (e^{(2k+1)}-e^{(2k+2)})\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2\
     &=2\underset{S}{\int} rac{\partial}{\partial n}(e^{(2k+1)}-e^{(2k+2)}) e^{(2k+1)}{\,	extrm d}\sigma - \|
abla (e^{(2k+1)}-e^{(2k+2)})\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2\
     &=2\underset{S}{\int} rac{\partial}{\partial n}(e^{(2k+1)}-e^{(2k+2)})( e^{(2k+1)}-e^{2k+2)}){\,	extrm d}\sigma - \|
abla (e^{(2k+1)}-e^{(2k+2)})\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2\
     &=2\underset{\Omega}{\int}|
abla (e^{(2k+1)}-e^{(2k+2)})|^2{\,	extrm d}x- \|
abla (e^{(2k+1)}-e^{(2k+2)})\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2\
     &=\|
abla (e^{(2k+1)}-e^{(2k+2)})\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2.
\end{align*}
Hence, for all $k\in {\mathbb N}\cup\{0\}$, we obtain the second key identity
 egin{equation}\label{14}
    \|
abla e^{(2k+1)}\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2- \|
abla e^{(2k+2)}\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2=\|
abla (e^{(2k+1)}-e^{(2k+2)})\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2.
\end{equation}
Together, \eqref{13} and \eqref{14} imply that
 egin{align*}
    \|
abla e^{(k)}\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2- \|
abla e^{(k+1)}\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2=\|
abla (e^{(k)}-e^{(k+1)})\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2 \hspace{4mm}	ext{ for all } k\in{\mathbb N}\cup\{0\}.
\end{align*}
Hence, $
abla e^{(k+1)}$ is orthogonal to $
abla(e^{(k)}-e^{(k+1)})$ $	ext{for all } k\in {\mathbb N}\cup \{0\}$.

label: Pr 3.1.3
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{Pr 3.1.3}
    Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a Hilbert space, and let $V_D$ and $V_N$ be closed subspaces of $\mathcal{H}$. Denote by $P_{V_D}$ and $P_{V_N}$ the orthogonal projections of $\mathcal{H}$ onto $V_D$ and $V_N$, respectively. Then, for every $x\in\mathcal{H}$,
    $$\underset{n\to\infty}{\text{lim}}\|(P_{V_D}\circ P_{V_N})^n(x)-P_{V_D\cap V_N}(x)\|_{\mathcal{H}}=0,$$
    where $P_{V_D\cap V_N}$ is the orthogonal projection of $\mathcal{H}$ onto the intersection $V_D\cap V_N$.

label: Pr A.1
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{Pr A.1}
    Let \ref{A_1} hold, and  $u\in H^1(\Omega)$ satisfy $$-\Delta u=f\hspace{8mm}\text{in}\hspace{2mm}\Omega,$$ where $f\in L^2(\Omega)$. If $\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}\big|_L\in H^{-\frac{1}{2}}(L)$ then $\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}\big|_S\in H^{-\frac{1}{2}}(S)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The following arguments are inspired by the proof of Proposition~1 in \cite{mazya}.\\
    Let $\varphi\in H^\frac{1}{2}(S)$ and define the functional $\mathcal{F}:H^\frac{1}{2}(S)\to {\mathbbm R}$ via
     $$\mathcal{F}(\varphi):=\underset{\Omega}{\int}(\nabla u\nabla \Tilde{\varphi}-f\Tilde{\varphi}){\,\textrm d}x-\underset{L}{\int}\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}\Tilde{\varphi}{\,\textrm d}\sigma,$$
    where $\Tilde{\varphi}\in H^1(\Omega)$ with $\Tilde{\varphi}|_S=\varphi$. If $\Tilde{\varphi}_1, \Tilde{\varphi}_2\in H^1(\Omega)$ with  $\Tilde{\varphi}_1=\Tilde{\varphi}_2$ on $S$, then
     $$\mathcal{F}((\Tilde{\varphi}_1-\Tilde{\varphi}_2)|_{S})=\underset{\Omega}{\int}\left(\nabla u\nabla(\Tilde{\varphi}_1-\Tilde{\varphi}_2)-f(\Tilde{\varphi}_1-\Tilde{\varphi}_2)\right){\,\textrm d}x-\underset{L}{\int}\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}(\Tilde{\varphi}_1-\Tilde{\varphi}_2){\,\textrm d}\sigma.$$
     Now, we use Green's formula to get
     \begin{align*}
         \mathcal{F}((\Tilde{\varphi}_1-\Tilde{\varphi}_2)|_{S})&=\underset{\Omega}{\int}f(\Tilde{\varphi}_1-\Tilde{\varphi}_2){\,\textrm d}x+\underset{L}{\int}\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}(\Tilde{\varphi}_1-\Tilde{\varphi}_2){\,\textrm d}\sigma-\underset{\Omega}{\int}f(\Tilde{\varphi}_1-\Tilde{\varphi}_2){\,\textrm d}x\\
         &\hspace{4mm}-\underset{L}{\int}\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}(\Tilde{\varphi}_1-\Tilde{\varphi}_2){\,\textrm d}\sigma\\
         &=0,\\
     \text{which implies }\mathcal{F}(\Tilde{\varphi}_1|_S)&=\mathcal{F}(\Tilde{\varphi}_2|_S).
     \end{align*}
     Hence, $\mathcal{{\mathcal F}}$ is well defined. ${\mathcal F}$ is  linear and continuous on $H^\frac{1}{2}(S)$. \\
     Taking $\varphi\in H^\frac{1}{2}(S)$, we get
     \begin{align*}
         \mathcal{F}(\varphi)&=\underset{\Omega}{\int}(\nabla u\nabla \Tilde{\varphi}-f\Tilde{\varphi}){\,\textrm d}x-\underset{L}{\int}\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}\Tilde{\varphi}{\,\textrm d}\sigma.
         \end{align*}
         Applying Green's formula, we can write the last result as follows
         \begin{align*}
         \mathcal{F}(\varphi)&=\underset{\Omega}{\int}f\Tilde{\varphi}{\,\textrm d}x+\underset{L}{\int}\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}\Tilde{\varphi}{\,\textrm d}\sigma+\underset{S}{\int}\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}\Tilde{\varphi}{\,\textrm d}\sigma-\underset{\Omega}{\int}f\Tilde{\varphi}{\,\textrm d}x-\underset{L}{\int}\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}\Tilde{\varphi}{\,\textrm d}\sigma\\
         &=\underset{S}{\int}\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}\Tilde{\varphi}{\,\textrm d}\sigma\\
         &=\underset{S}{\int}\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}\Big|_S\varphi{\,\textrm d}\sigma\\
         \text{implies } \mathcal{F}&=\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}\Big|_S.
     \end{align*}
     Since ${\mathcal F}$ is a linear and continuous function on $H^\frac{1}{2}(S)$ and $\mathcal{F}=\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}\Big|_S$ , it implies that
     $$\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}\Big|_S\in H^{-\frac{1}{2}}(S).$$

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $\Omega\subset{\mathbbm R}^d$ be a bounded domain. A function $u\in H^1(\Omega)$ is said to be weakly harmonic in $\Omega$ (or $-\Delta u=0$ weakly in $\Omega$) if 
    $$\underset{\Omega}{\int}\nabla u\nabla \Psi{\,\textrm d}x=0\hspace{1cm}\text{for all }\Psi\in H_0^1(\Omega).$$
    We refer the reader to \cite{Liang} for a discussion of weakly harmonic functions.
head: environment

label: Th A.1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Th A.1}
     Let $S\neq\emptyset$. If $u\in H^1(\Omega)$ is weakly harmonic in $\Omega$ and  satisfies  
   $$u=0\hspace{6mm}\text{on}\hspace{2mm} S,$$
and
    $$ \frac{\partial u}{\partial n}=0\hspace{6mm}\text{on}\hspace{2mm} S,$$
then $u=0$ in $\Omega$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: See Theorem~1.4 in \cite{mikko}.

label: Pr A.2
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{Pr A.2}
    $V_D$ and $V_N$ are subspaces of $\mathcal{H}$, where $V_D$, $V_N$, and $\mathcal{H}$ are defined in Section \ref{sec 3.2}. Then $V_D$ and $V_N$ are closed subspaces in $\mathcal{H}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $v$ be the limit point of $V_D$. Take $(v_n)\subset V_D$ such that $$v_n\to v\hspace{4mm} \text{in}\hspace{2mm} \mathcal{H}.$$
    It suffices to show that $v\in V_D$.\\
     For $\phi\in H_0^1(\Omega)$ and $v_n\in V_D$, we have
    $$\underset{\Omega}{\int}\nabla v_n\nabla \phi{\,\textrm d}x=0.$$
    Since $v_n\to v$ in $\mathcal{H}$, it follows that
    $$\underset{\Omega}{\int}\nabla v\nabla \phi{\,\textrm d}x=0\hspace{6mm}\text{for all }\phi\in H_0^1(\Omega).$$
    Hence, $v$ is weakly harmonic.
    Furthermore,  $v_n=0$ on $S$ in the trace sense for every $n\in {\mathbb N}$. By the continuity of the trace operator, it follows that $v=\underset{n\to\infty}{\text{lim}}v_n=0$ on $S$ in the trace sense.\\
    Hence, $V_D$ is a closed subspace in $\mathcal{H}$.\\
    Now, let $w$ be the limit point of $V_N$. Take $(w_n)\subset V_N$ such that $$w_n\to w\hspace{4mm}\text{in}\hspace{2mm} \mathcal{H}.$$
     It suffices to show that $w\in V_N$.\\
    For $\psi\in H_{DL}^1(\Omega)$ and $w_n\in V_N$, we have
    $$\underset{\Omega}{\int}\nabla w_n\nabla \psi{\,\textrm d}x=0.$$
    Since $w_n\to w$ in $\mathcal{H}$, it follows that
    $$\underset{\Omega}{\int}\nabla w\nabla \psi{\,\textrm d}x=0\hspace{6mm}\text{for all }\psi\in H_{DL}^1(\Omega).$$
    Hence, $w$ is weakly harmonic and $\frac{\partial w}{\partial n}=0$ on $S$.\\
    Therefore, $V_N$ is a closed subspace in $\mathcal{H}$.
